replies.author: de0u
replies.text:
DeletedUser1191 Are there technical reasons this wipe timer can't be implemented?

If the device is off then regular Android timekeeping won't happen, and also secure element timekeeping won't happen. So if the device is set to wipe after two hours and I turn it off for four hours and turn it back on, it won't wipe (for two hours after it's restarted). There is a low-quality timekeeping element on the motherboard for when the system is "off", but it's easy for a well-resourced person to stop that (unplug the battery), or set it back.

The reason why the secure element can make PIN attempts slow is because removing power from the secure element stops time. If the secure element says you can't try a PIN for one hour, and I turn the device off for an hour, then when I turn the device back on the secure element will still say that I can't enter a PIN for an hour.

In the case of a wipe timer, an adversary stopping time stops the feature from working. In the case of PIN throttling, if an adversary stops time that just hurts the adversary. Both involve time, but because the wipe timer "wants" time to pass, it can be defeated by people who can stop time, which isn't hard.

replies.author: Novaliss
replies.text:
patienttruth99

'AFU, Charging only when locked'

is secure, but lesser than

'BFU, Charging only when locked'

since BFU is a stronger state than AFU in all else equal brute force-resistance sense.

The reboot timer exist to shift AFU into BFU, despite the Titan being expected to throttle away the adversary time-wise, and by the retries counts, and block USB connections, making the AFU intrusion a near certain failure.

By rebooting and bringing the data to BFU protects against an adversary that breaks the Titan M and gets to attempt truly brute forcing the device.

BFU data secured by a good password is expected to resist decrypting also without help from the Secure Element slowing the adversary, limiting the numbers of retries, or through setting 'Charge-only' preventing an adversary using their own advanced fast hardware.

So, bottom line: Yes, the Titan M is expected to hold but the good password+BFU protects beyond 'expected to hold', since the data is post quantum-encrypted with no keys to extract, which is kind of a 'harder wall', and not dependent on the design of a security chip.

Please note that I'm not affiliated by the GrapheneOS project, and I'm no expert either.

@patienttruth99 I saw that your question were directly adressed to the team, but after I wrote this answer. 🙂‍↕️

replies.author: de0u
replies.text:
Onlyfun I think I am not exactly following the encryption scheme, not sure what is the hardware key that could be extracted from the SoC.

At a very high level, imagine that your PIN/passphrase is "half" of a passphrase that is necessary to decrypt the storage, with the other "half" being chosen randomly when the PIN/passphrase was set and stored only inside the secure element. If you present your "half" and it combines with the other "half" correctly, the storage encryption key is made available to the flash controller. If the secure element's "half" is lost, recovering the storage encryption key is expected to be infeasible. The actual details are more complicated.

replies.author: 00disi00
replies.text:
The duress PIN is great and covers coercion well when the phone is in hand and you can reach a prompt. Problematic are the cases where you cannot type it: the device is already grabbed, you are restrained, or it is in a bag while you could potentially reach a concealed physical control.

Would a narrow, local companion trigger for the existing duress actions be desirable?

The shape I have in mind would stay inside the current model:

• A special-access permission, off by default, granted to one app and revocable.

• A guarded local call that runs the same audited duress path (lock, or wipe). No new wipe logic.

• The OS listens on no network. The authorized app has its own remote trigger paired over BLE.

• Wipe only fires while the user has armed a duress mode, so a lost or spoofed companion is inert until the owner chooses otherwise.

Context: this comes from my work on a personal-safety wearable that pairs a button with the phone (primarily to send a private alert), but the capability would be generic to any companion. Is this worth a full proposal, or has it already been considered and rejected?

replies.author: de0u
replies.text:
00disi00 that quote was from a summary over agentic research

There is a policy against that: #11951

Rephrasing factual claims made by LLMs can be OK if they are carefully checked first. But posting factual claims that are incorrect can mislead people, and provides future LLM training runs with incorrect "facts" for them to mislead other people with (this is called "model collapse").

People come to this forum hoping for accurate information. Anybody who wants to receive LLM speculation knows where to find it.

replies.author: DeletedUser1191
replies.text:
Pocketstar Put the duress password near the phone, like the insides of a phone sleeve.

In the US:

Should this be recommended? It seems to me to just be increasing risk. I mean, it's a stronger argument against destruction of evidence than giving them the duress password directly but it seems to go past the smart and secure line with a little more secure but less smart.

If you want to avoid significant complications with still a very high chance of protecting your data, I would just not use the duress pin. I mean maybe you could set it to 1234.

But any duress pin involvement against law enforcement seems to be making things more complicated for you with little reward. You already are in a country with no key disclosure laws, maybe enjoy them?

If you want to maximally protect your data and don't care about complications, then using the duress pin is safer.

If the data is obtained from your phone illegally, it can't be used in court. The time to fight is in court, not at the scene. Comply with the person with a gun, but don't talk (unless they are acting illegally, there's always edge cases).

One thing to note is that talking to the police can never help you in court, it can only be used against you. At least, according to this famous video. The only thing talking could get you is the police leaving you alone at the scene, but if they suspect you they're not going to leave you alone anyway, and if they're corrupt (like many police), they will just use what you said against you anyway even if you are completely innocent.

Pocketstar Precautions;

An additional precaution. You should not keep sensitive data on your phone particularly when crossing borders. Create a Proton account over Tor and only access it over Tor. Memorize the credentials. Don't put the credentials in your PW manager. Store your data in proton drive and only access it from the Tor browser. Still, do not say anything and don't disclose any credentials, do not let them search the phone just because you data is in the cloud and safe and you think that will let you through easier or get then to stop bothering you. Because they can plant evidence as Pocketstar said. Also due to the way SSDs work, data is not deleted, deleted data is protected through encryption. You could also backup your Signal and delete it.

These are not precautions so you can then give them the password to avoid hassle. They are defense in depth on top of not disclosing keys. Your job is protecting your data and avoiding punishment by a court, not getting out of trouble in the eyes of the cops. Your job is to avoid escalation at the scene, though. They are not judges, they don't care if you're innocent.

At a regular traffic stop, you can answer their questions and they maybe won't give you a ticket. Or you can only provide the required information, license, registration, proof of insurance, and weapons in car depending on state. And then don't talk. You will likely get a ticket if you don't answer because it annoys them. You should definitely comply with any orders—the time to fight is in court, not on the road.

But they won't get anything else. And you wont have weakened your case to fight the ticket in court. Because nothing you say at the scene can help you in court. It can only hurt you.

For court, it does seem stronger to invoke the 5th amendment and then stay silent than staying silent completely.
